# Bernese Mountain Dog Grooming Guide: Managing That Beautiful, Heavy Coat

*By Sarah Mitchell, Certified Master Groomer (CMG), International Professional Groomers Inc.*

---

If you own a Bernese Mountain Dog, you already know two things: they are the sweetest dogs alive, and they shed enough hair to knit a small sweater every week. The Berner's tri-color coat — jet black, rust, and white — is one of the most striking in the dog world, but it requires consistent maintenance to keep it healthy, mat-free, and manageable.

Here's everything you need to know about grooming your Bernese Mountain Dog, whether you're handling it at home or working with a professional groomer.

## Understanding the Bernese Mountain Dog Coat

Berners have a double coat: a longer, slightly wavy or straight outer coat and a thick, woolly undercoat. That undercoat is the source of most of the shedding — and it's substantial. Twice a year (spring and fall), Berners go through a "coat blow" where the undercoat sheds heavily. During those periods, daily brushing is not an exaggeration.

The good news: Berner coats don't require trimming to a specific breed standard length the way poodles or spaniels do. The bad news: they mat easily, particularly behind the ears, under the front legs (armpits), and around the collar area.

## Brushing: The Most Important Part of Berner Grooming

**How often:** 2–3 times per week minimum; daily during shedding season.

**What to use:**
- A slicker brush to remove loose hair and detangle the outer coat
- An undercoat rake or deshedding tool (like a FURminator) to pull out loose undercoat
- A wide-tooth metal comb to check for mats you may have missed

Always brush in the direction of hair growth, working section by section. Pay extra attention to the "friction zones" — behind the ears, armpits, groin, and collar line. These areas mat first because they experience constant movement and moisture.

If you encounter a mat, don't pull through it. Apply a detangling spray, gently work the edges apart with your fingers, then use a mat splitter or slicker brush to work from the outside of the mat inward.

## Bathing Your Bernese Mountain Dog

**How often:** Every 6–8 weeks for a dog that's not getting into mud regularly. Active outdoor Berners may need baths more frequently.

Bathing a Berner is a project — they're large (70–115 lbs) and that double coat holds water. A few tips:

- Use a high-velocity dryer after the bath to blow water out of the undercoat before towel drying. Air-drying a Berner takes hours and can lead to "hot spots" — irritated skin under damp fur.
- Use a moisturizing dog shampoo; the Berner coat can dry out with harsh formulas.
- Make sure you rinse thoroughly. Shampoo residue trapped in a double coat causes itching and skin irritation.

For most owners, bathing a Berner is easier done at a self-wash station (many grooming shops and pet stores offer these) rather than a home bathtub.

## Professional Grooming for Berners

**How often:** Every 8–12 weeks.

A professional groom for a Berner typically includes:
- Thorough deshedding treatment (often with a high-velocity dryer)
- Bath and blow-dry
- Brush-out
- Nail trim
- Ear cleaning
- Trimming of the paw pads and any feathering that gets unruly

Berners don't need a "haircut" per se — their coats are kept natural. But professional groomers have the tools and technique to do a deep deshed that significantly reduces the amount of loose hair your dog carries around (and deposits on your couch).

When looking for a groomer for your Berner, ask whether they have experience with double-coated, large-breed dogs. Not all grooming shops are set up for 100-lb dogs, and high-velocity dryers are a must for efficient results.

## Common Grooming Mistakes Berner Owners Make

**Shaving the coat.** It's tempting when shedding is overwhelming, but shaving a double coat doesn't stop shedding — it damages the coat's natural insulation and can cause regrowth problems. The coat may never grow back quite right. Let a groomer do a thorough deshed instead.

**Skipping brushing between baths.** Mats form fast on Berners, especially in humid weather. A week without brushing can mean an hour of mat removal.

**Neglecting the ears.** Berner ears are floppy and can trap moisture and debris. Check weekly and clean with a vet-approved ear cleaner.

## Finding a Groomer for Your Berner

Because of their size and coat complexity, Berners benefit from groomers who specialize in large, double-coated breeds. When you search for a dog groomer near you, look for one who lists "double coat" or "deshedding treatments" in their services — this signals they have the right equipment and experience for your dog.

Bernese Mountain Dogs are high-maintenance in the grooming department, but the payoff is a dog that looks like it belongs on a Swiss mountain postcard. With a solid routine and the right professional help, that coat stays gorgeous year-round.
